question: Term life for young families in Moorpark and Simi Valley: how much is enough?
dek: A plain-talk guide for Moorpark and Simi Valley parents on how to size a term life policy so it covers the mortgage, replaces income, and lasts as long as the family actually needs it.
answer: For most young families in Moorpark, Simi Valley, and the broader Conejo Valley and Ventura County area, a term life policy sized at roughly ten to twelve times gross household income, plus the outstanding mortgage balance, covers the two biggest financial holes a death leaves behind. A 20 or 30 year term usually lines up better with a long mortgage and young children than a shorter term does. Group coverage through work is a real benefit, but it almost never replaces enough income on its own, and it disappears the moment you change jobs. Getting those numbers right while you are young and healthy is the single most cost-effective move a growing family can make.

sections.h: Start with two numbers: income replacement and the mortgage
p: When I sit down with a young family, I ask two questions first. What would your household need each year to stay afloat without your paycheck? And what is left on your mortgage? In Ventura County, home prices have pushed loan balances well into the six figures for most buyers, so the mortgage number alone can be significant. A common starting point is to multiply your annual income by ten to twelve and then add whatever remains on the loan. That combined figure is the floor, not the ceiling. Childcare, college savings, and a surviving spouse who may need time before returning to work full time can push the right number higher.

The mortgage piece matters a lot to me personally because my wife works in probate real estate. She sees what happens when a homeowner dies without enough coverage. The surviving spouse sometimes has to sell the house quickly just to cover expenses, and if the estate has to go through probate first, that process can take many months in Ventura County. A life insurance payout, by contrast, goes directly to a named beneficiary and bypasses probate entirely. That speed and simplicity can be the difference between keeping the family home and losing it.

sections.h: Match the term length to your kids and your loan
p: Term length is where I see families make the most common mistake. They pick a 10 year term because it is cheaper, but their youngest child is two years old and their mortgage runs another 28 years. If something happens in year 11, the family is unprotected. A 20 or 30 year term costs more per month, but it keeps coverage in place through the years that actually carry risk: while children are at home, while the mortgage balance is still large, and while a surviving spouse has not yet had time to rebuild savings.

For a couple in their late 20s or early 30s buying in Moorpark or Simi Valley, a 30 year term often makes the most sense. It runs to or past the mortgage payoff date, it covers the children all the way through college, and it locks in a rate while you are young and likely healthy. If your situation changes and you no longer need the full coverage later, you can always let a policy lapse or reduce it. You cannot go back and buy the same coverage cheaply at 50 if your health has changed.

sections.h: Why work coverage alone usually falls short
p: Most employers offer group term life insurance at one or two times your annual salary. That sounds helpful, and it is, but it leaves a wide gap compared to the ten to twelve times income benchmark most families actually need. On a $100,000 salary, one times coverage is $100,000. The mortgage alone on a Ventura County home often dwarfs that number.

There is a second problem that many people in the Conejo Valley do not think about until it is too late: group coverage is tied to your job. If you are laid off, change careers, or leave to start a business, that coverage ends. An individual term policy belongs to you regardless of where you work. Think of work coverage as a supplement to your own policy, not a substitute for it. If your employer offers additional voluntary coverage at good rates, that can be a smart add-on, but the foundation should be a policy you own and control.
